IMAGING: • Small or absent stomach bubble
○ Often difficult to define when stomach is "small"
○ Stomach size varies in same fetus over several hours
○ Requires follow-up scans on questionable cases
• Pouch sign
○ Transient filling of proximal esophagus with swallowing
○ Perform focused exam of neck and upper chest
○ Fetal MR helpful in difficult/equivocal cases
• Fetal growth restriction seen in up to 40%
• Polyhydramnios
○ Rarely develops before 20 weeks
○ Fetal swallowing not important part of amniotic fluid
dynamics until that time

○ Aneuploidy reported in 5-44% (trisomy 18 and 21)

dysmotility, anastomotic stricture, recurrent TEF

polyhydramnios

up scans in setting of small stomach
• Do not confuse normal pharynx with esophageal pouch

IMAGING: • Normal small bowel < 7-mm diameter
• Echogenic bowel in 2nd trimester may be 1st sign of atresia

○ Triple bubble for proximal jejunal atresia
○ Sausage-shaped bowel loops
• Hyperperistalsis of obstructed segments in real time
• Polyhydramnios more likely with proximal atresia
○ Usually develops after 26 weeks
• At risk for perforation and meconium peritonitis
○ More common with ileal obstruction
• Consider fetal MR to better delineate site of obstruction
• Increasing complexity of bowel contents by US, and higher
signal on T1 MR, correlate with more distal obstructions
• Obtain sonographic views of rectum/anus to rule out anal
atresia

• Frequently associated with other GI anomalies

• Long-term outcome dependent on length of resected
bowel and associated malformations
○ Long-term sequelae include short gut syndrome,
dysmotility, and functional obstruction
• Testing for cystic fibrosis is recommended in all cases of
distal obstruction, as meconium ileus may have identical
appearance

PATHOLOGY: ○ Overgrowth syndrome with predisposition to childhood
tumors, particularly Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma
○ Macroglossia is most consistent fetal finding
CLINICAL ISSUES: • ~ 5% of fetal tumors occur in liver, and most are benign
○ Congenital hepatic hemangioma, mesenchymal
hamartoma
• Malignant fetal liver tumors are rare
○ Consider hepatoblastoma for large, solitary mass
○ Consider leukemia in fetus with trisomy 21 and
hepatosplenomegaly
○ Always carefully evaluate liver for metastases in cases of
neuroblastoma
